records.text: Fork. One piece is now hitting several targets at once, and the other side has some sorting out to do.
The other side gets a fork out of this. One of their pieces can reach several targets in a single move.
Another move had a fork going, one piece against several targets. This move leaves that on the table.
Pinned to the king. That piece now holds its line whether it likes it or not; moving off would expose the king behind it.
Now the other side has a pin against the king to work with. A pinned piece holds its line or the king is exposed.
A pin to the king was on offer in another move, freezing a piece on its line. This move passes it up.
Skewered. The front piece is under attack, and once it moves aside, whatever stood behind it on that line is exposed.
A skewer is now on offer to the other side. If the front piece moves off the line, whatever stands behind it may be exposed.
Another move had a skewer ready: move the front piece, and whatever stood behind it would have been exposed.
Capture the guard, and whatever it was guarding stands bare. That is the whole point of the move.
One of the defenders can now be captured. Whatever it guards may lose its protection along with it.
Another move would have removed a defender and stripped its charge of cover. Here that defender is left in place.
Its own pieces have the king boxed in. The back rank is where this move collects.
The king's own pieces are sitting on its escape squares. The other side now has a back-rank mate to aim for.
Another move had a back-rank mate, against a king stuck behind its own pieces. This move strolls on by.
This pawn is running for the last rank, where it turns into a new piece. Promotion is the threat.
A pawn of theirs is now in the running for promotion. Pawns that reach the last rank stop being pawns.
A stronger move cleared a pawn's way to promotion. This move keeps that road closed.
One piece clears the line, and the piece it was screening gets to attack. Discovered attack, textbook.
One of their pieces is standing in front of another. If it moves, the piece behind gets a clear line. A discovered attack, available to them.
Another move would have unmasked an attack by shifting the piece in front. This move leaves the mask on.
One move, carrying two demands. A double attack, and each demand needs an answer.
The other side can make two threats with a single move now. A double attack, and both will need answering.
A stronger move would have hit two targets in a single turn. This move leaves that double attack unplayed.
Deflection: a defender gets hauled away, and whatever it was covering now stands unguarded.
One defender is doing a vital job. The other side can now drag it away from that job: a deflection, theirs to use.
Another move would have pried a defender loose from its job. That chance at deflection goes begging.
That piece has no guard at all. Take it. Nothing more complicated than that.
An undefended piece was available to another move. This one leaves it standing. Loose pieces get billed.
This leaves a piece hanging, free for the other side to take. They will not need an invitation.
A piece is there for the taking now. This move walked its only real defender off the job. Costly, that.
A piece is now open to capture. The opponent's last move made a threat, and this move lets it stand.
The capture looks fine until the recapture, which takes a more valuable piece. An exchange is judged at the end, not the start.
A minor piece is developed, off its starting square and working.
The alternative developed a minor piece instead.
Open file, rook on it. Not a pawn of either color on the whole file.
The alternative was a rook on an open file, a file without a single pawn.
The rook now works a semi-open file: none of its own pawns there, at least one of the enemy's.
A semi-open file was available to a rook with another move: its own pawns gone from the file, an enemy pawn still there.
That pawn is passed; no enemy pawn stands in front of it on its file or either neighbor. Worth watching.
A passed pawn was available to another move, free of enemy pawns ahead on its file and both neighbors.
One step closer to the last rank for the passed pawn.
The alternative pushed the passed pawn forward, nearer the last rank.
That pawn is isolated now. No friendly pawn on either neighboring file to keep it company.
Another move would have left an isolated pawn, without a friendly pawn on either file beside it.
That piece was on its own. Not anymore; it has a guard.
Covering the loose piece was the alternative. Cheap insurance.
This piece has no defender now. Undefended is a condition, not a verdict.
With another move, a piece would have stood undefended. By itself, that would not have cost it.
An escape square opens up for the king, legal and available. Escape routes are cheaper to build before they are needed.
The alternative gave the king a fresh legal flight square.
Castling done: the king steps aside and the rook comes into play; two pieces moved, one tempo spent.
The alternative was castling, which shifts king and rook with a single move.
With this capture, one side's bishop pair is history. It keeps bishops on only one color now.
The alternative took a bishop and split up the other side's pair.
Two pawns of one color on one file: doubled.
Another move would have left doubled pawns, two of one color stacked on a single file.
Forced checkmate is now available to the other side. The defense around the king has run out. Follow the mating line from here.
There was a forced mate in the position. This move passes it up. Unfinished business.
The material is on offer, and taking it does not refute the sacrifice, not in the line searched. The offer has teeth.
Every other searched move was losing. This one kept the game playable. No room for anything else.
This move holds on to the advantage. Nothing else searched did; the rest were losing.
The reply has a capture available immediately. Check what it costs.
The best answer for the other side gives check. Everything else waits until the king is dealt with.
The engine prefers a different move. Put the two side by side and compare the replies; that is where they differ.
This costs something against the engine's best move. The reply presents the bill.
Strong, and economical about it. Next to anything the engine searched, almost nothing is conceded.
Sound. The engine has a preference, but most of the value is still there.
The human-move model predicts this one. The engine has a stronger move, and the reply shows why. Tempting moves have replies too.
The human-move model would not have picked this. The engine rates it strong, and it holds up.
One searched move kept the position playable. This was not it. The human-move model rates that defense hard to find.
The engine's best, and a hard find according to the human-move model and the alternatives searched. Worth filing away.
The position holds, and this move is why. The human-move model and the searched alternatives say it was hard to see. Found anyway.
Predicted by the human-move model, ranked first by the engine. Convenient.
A likely move, according to the human-move model. The engine calls it strong, with another move above it.
Before this move, the clock was nearly empty. That is context, nothing more.
Played fast, and the clock still had plenty.
A long think, and the clock paid for it.
Theory knows this line. Known territory, for now.
Theory runs out here. No more book past this point; calculation from here on.
The earlier setback has been dealt with. With this move, the position is playable again.
The earlier setback no longer decides things; the position is playable again. Their errors helped. Help is help.
The opponent's last move opened a gap. This move cashes it in. As it should.
The opponent's last move put something on the table. This move leaves it there.
This issue already turned up earlier in the game. Same warning sign, again. Compare those moments.
The earlier unguarded piece has its guard back. Repaired.
No single disaster. Small concessions, one after another, and this is another one. They add up.
The advantage stayed in hand right up to the recorded win. Converted, without handing any of it back.
The same issue is on file in other saved games. It has a history. Study them together.
Mate, and final. Not one legal move left for that king.
It ends in checkmate, the king without a legal move. The lesson sits earlier, in the defense.
Drawn. Nobody collects. The earlier decisions are still worth a look.
Take in the position. Then move.
That fails. Check the reply before trusting the next attempt.
That attempt returned nothing. Enter the move a second time.
The saved engine analysis has a forced checkmate here, for the side that made this move.
After this move, the saved engine analysis has a forced checkmate. For the other side.
When the saved line is over, the side that made this move has gained material, measured against the start of that line.
When the saved line is over, the side that made this move has lost material, measured against the start of that line.
This exercise accepts the move. No clear tactical reason shows in the moves given, so none is claimed.
No acceptance for this move in this exercise. No clear tactical reason shows in the moves given, and none is invented.
This matches a saved answer. For this exercise, the saved answers decide.
This move matches no saved answer. That makes it wrong for the exercise, not necessarily bad chess.
Run through the move again. After that, the next position.
That move is good. Keep the reason attached to it.
Practice saved, review schedule untouched.
Solved, though the relearning mark stays.
The starting position, before any of these moves are played.
Moving on. Look at what changed.
Check, and it gets answered before anything else.
With this move, the check is dealt with.
The pawn reaches the last rank and is promoted.
Promotion, with check attached.
The pawn promotes, and that is mate. Every move the king had is gone.
The pawn promotes, and the same move takes its own king out of check.
Something gets taken.
Takes a piece, gives check.
Takes a piece and mates. Every legal move the king had is gone.
Takes a piece, and the check is escaped by the same move.
The pawn takes on the last rank and becomes a new piece.
The pawn takes on the last rank, promotes, and checks the king, all with a single move.
Capturing onto the last rank, the pawn promotes, and that is mate.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, taking its own king out of check in the process.
The king castles, and the move gives check.
Castling delivers mate; the enemy king has no legal move.
The forking piece hits several targets and collects one. Here the fork ends with a net material gain.
That piece is not allowed to make the capture: it is pinned, and leaving the line would leave its own king in check, which is illegal.
The attacked piece cannot simply run, because its king sits behind it on the line. Whatever it does, the king has to stay covered.
No recapture is available: every defender is pinned against its king. In the line shown, material is won.
Stepping off its line would expose the king, so the pinned piece stays put. It does not survive these moves.
The front piece gets out of the way. Then the piece behind it gets taken, down the same line.
Check moves the king off the line by force. The same attacker then helps itself to the piece that stood behind.
Step one: the lone defender comes off. Later in these moves, whatever it guarded follows.
The defender is pulled off its job, and the piece it left is taken.
The blocker moves. Another piece captures down the line it opened.
One piece moves aside, unmasking a check from the piece it was hiding.
That is double check: two attackers on the king, and only a king move answers that.
The moving piece attacks once and unmasks a second attack. Here the second piece collects its target.
The pawn promotes, and that side finishes this example with a net material gain.
A piece nobody guarded comes off the board. The side that took it ends the example up material, net.
The attacking piece was held in a relative pin until the opponent's previous move released it. Nobody moved the target after that, and by the end of the line shown, it is gone.
The marked reply belongs to the other side. Put it on the board and watch what it does.
Before any move, list the pieces that could be taken without a useful recapture.
Before a quiet move, look for enemy pieces nobody is guarding.
Look at forcing moves where one piece hits two valuable targets.
A pinned piece is guarding whatever sits behind it. Check that price before it moves.
The first target may be a screen. A valuable piece behind it makes a skewer.
Before trading off a defender, know exactly what it protects.
When a blocking piece moves, follow every line it uncovers.
Hunt for a move carrying two demands. Checks and newly opened lines count.
Before a back-rank defender moves, know where the king can escape.
Count the moves between the pawn and promotion. Then check every forcing push.
A defender that moves takes its protection with it. Know what that covers first.
First, the value the capture wins. Then, the value the recapture takes back. The difference is the price.
Check whether a forcing exchange can drag a defender off something else it guards.
Saved answers set the rules of this exercise. Plenty of other legal moves are still good chess.
This line assumes strong replies. Not all of them are forced.
Material changes cover the shown line only, counted from its start. The written explanation lists the piece values.
The saved line has no simple tactical reason to offer. Play through it and weigh each reply. No positional story is assumed.
This explanation follows the exercise's saved answer policy. The written notes show which setting is in force.
These are the moves of the opening line under study.
Correct; the selected study material includes that move.
Any move from the selected study lines will do. Play one.
Several moves from the selected opening lines count here. One will do.
The selected study material has one move for this position. Find it.
Not one of the selected opening lines. Another attempt.
Not in the selected opening lines; try another. This saved attempt leaves the changed study's review schedule alone.
Not in the selected opening lines; try another. The position is retired, so nothing about its review schedule changes.
In mixed Due, this line's moves are accepted. In dedicated practice, it is asked for by itself.
Scheduled recalls want the moves of the side that was selected. When active studies share a position, they share a single card.
Reload the saved session first, then play on.
Here is the verified line, move by move on the board.
Marked as revealed. The solution is below, ready to replay.
Solved, second attempt. The miss stays on record, and so does the finish.
Full solution, not one wrong move. Clean work.
Not the solution. Everything correct before it stays saved.
Correct so far. There is another move to find.
No hurry. Calculate first. Then move.
Not enough from the engine to explain this position, and no invented explanation in its place. Exploring the board is still allowed.
Review on hold. Pick it back up below, or try a move on the board.
Pick a move to review, or move a piece to try another path.
Book move, this: a recognized opening has it on file.
The opening line is a known one, and this move is part of it.
Theory has seen this move before; it belongs to a recognized opening.
Still theory.
Theory covers this one too.
The reply is straight from theory too.
The line continues by the book.
Known moves, still.
The book supplies one more.
No departure yet.
Theory still. A name, not a verdict.
The other side has a forced checkmate after this. A natural pick for the human-move model. Natural does not mean safe.
Mate was available, by force. The human-move model expects this move instead, and the mate goes uncollected.
The reply can take something on the spot. To the human-move model, the move looks ordinary. The reply does not care.
This gives up value against the engine's best. The human-move model calls it a natural choice; the reply sends the bill.
One of their pieces is now in range of several targets at once, which is a fork. Natural, by the human-move model, and the fork is real either way.
A skewer is there for the other side: if the front piece steps aside, whatever stands behind it may be exposed. The human-move model finds the move ordinary.
Every other searched move was losing. This one, and only this one, survives. The human-move model rates it a hard defense to see. Found anyway.
Nothing but this kept the position playable; the other searched moves lost. The human-move model and the alternatives make it a hard find.
Without this move, the advantage was gone; everything else searched was losing. The human-move model rates this one hard to see. Precise work.
No other searched move kept the advantage; each one lost. The human-move model and the alternatives put this among the hard finds.
A fork: one piece, and several things to lose. The human-move model did not predict it. The engine grades it strong.
One piece now has several targets in reach. A fork, and the engine's best move. The human-move model says it was not easy to find.
A pin to the king; step off the line and the king is exposed, so the piece stays. Unexpected, to the human-move model. Strong, to the engine.
A pin holds a piece to its king. The engine ranks the move best, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Sharp.
A piece is up for grabs now; this move walked off and left it without its only real defender. Natural, by the human-move model, and still costly.

Its only real defender gone, a piece is there for the other side to capture. One searched move kept the position playable, and this was not that move. The human-move model rates that defense hard to find.
A piece is open to capture now. The opponent's last move brought a threat, and this move lets it stand. To the human-move model, it is an ordinary move.
The threat from the opponent's last move still stands, and a piece is open to capture. Only one searched move held, and it was not this one; the human-move model calls that defense hard to see.
On the recapture, a more valuable piece goes. The human-move model sees an ordinary capture. Count to the end of the exchange.
This capture lets a more valuable piece be taken back. The only searched move that kept the position playable was different, and the human-move model rates it hard to find.
A fork: one attacker, several things to lose. Predicted by the human-move model, ranked first by the engine.
Several targets, one attacker, which makes it a fork. Predicted by the human-move model. The engine grades it strong and keeps another move above it.
The other side gets a fork, one of their pieces reaching several targets. Exactly one searched move kept the position playable; this was not it, and the human-move model rates it hard to find.
There was a fork in another move. The human-move model finds this one more natural, and the fork stays on the shelf.
The only searched move that kept the position playable was a fork, one piece hitting several targets. Nobody played it. The human-move model grades it hard to find.
Pinned to its king, that piece is stuck on its line. The human-move model predicts it; the engine puts nothing above it.
The pin keeps a piece fixed to its king's line. Likely, says the human-move model. Strong, says the engine, with a preference elsewhere.
A pin against the king is now on the table for the other side. Pinned, a piece holds its line or the king is exposed. To the human-move model, the move is ordinary.
A pin to the king is now available to the other side. A single searched move held elsewhere, and the human-move model rates it hard to find.
A stronger move pinned a piece to its king. The human-move model finds this move more natural. The pin goes unused.
The only searched move that held used a pin to the king. Not played. The human-move model rates it a hard find.
Skewer: the front piece gets out of the way, and what it was shielding is laid bare. The engine's best. The human-move model and the alternatives rate it hard to find.
Skewer: move the front piece, and the piece behind it is next in line. Not a move the human-move model predicts. Strong, all the same, by the engine.
Two pieces, one line, one skewer. Natural for the human-move model, first for the engine.
Skewered, front to back. The human-move model expects it; the engine calls it strong and prefers another.

A skewer is now on offer to the other side: the front piece moves, and whatever stands behind it may be exposed. One searched move kept the position playable, and this was not it. The human-move model rates it hard to see.
A skewer sat in another move: shift the front piece, expose what is behind it. The human-move model finds this move natural, and the skewer goes unplayed.
The only searched move that held had a skewer in it. This move did something else. The human-move model grades it hard to see.
The defender is taken, and whatever it protected stands bare. The engine's best, and the human-move model and the searched alternatives put it among the hard finds.
Capture the defender, and what it guarded is left without cover. The human-move model would have passed it over; the engine calls it strong.
The defender comes off, and what it guarded is left to fend for itself. The likely move for the human-move model, and the engine's first choice.
Removing a defender strips its protection away. Likely, by the human-move model. Strong, by the engine, which ranks another move higher.
One of the defenders can now be captured, and whatever it guards could find itself unwatched. The human-move model predicts this move.
A defender is now there to be captured. Only one searched move held, and it was not this one; the human-move model calls that defense hard to find.
Another move would have removed a defender, protection and all. The human-move model finds this move more natural. The defender stays on duty.
The only searched move that held captured a defender. It went unplayed, and the human-move model rates it hard to find.
The back rank is the target; the king is boxed in by its own pieces. Best, in the engine's view; hard to find, in the human-move model's.
Its own pieces fence the king in, and the back rank is the target. Low on the human-move model's list, and strong in the engine's search.
A king hemmed in by its own pieces, and a back-rank mate aimed at it. The human-move model and the engine land on the same move: natural, and best.
The king's own pieces are sitting on its exits, and this move goes after the back rank. The human-move model finds it ordinary. Strong for the engine, not first.
The pawn has a road to promotion. The engine ranks it best, and the human-move model grades it a hard find.
This sends a pawn toward promotion. Not one the human-move model predicts. Strong all the same, in the engine's view.
That pawn is making for the last rank. No disagreement: the human-move model predicts it, and the engine ranks it first.
The pawn wants the last rank. The human-move model finds the move natural; the engine calls it strong and prefers another.
One of their pawns now has a route to promotion. Likely, by the human-move model. The pawn is the problem either way.
Promotion is now a real option for the other side. Only one searched move kept the position playable, and this move was not it; the human-move model rates it hard to find.
Another move opened a pawn's road to promotion. The human-move model finds this one more natural. The road stays shut.
The only searched move that held pushed a pawn toward promotion. Not played. The human-move model rates it a hard find.
A blocker steps aside, and the piece it was hiding gets to attack. A discovered attack, and the engine's best. The human-move model rates it hard to see.
The blocker moves, and the attack behind it opens. Unexpected, to the human-move model. Strong, to the engine.
A discovered attack: one piece moves off the line and unmasks the piece behind. Predicted by the human-move model, ranked first by the engine.
A discovered attack opens behind the moving piece. The human-move model finds it natural; strong, by the engine, with another move ranked higher.
One of their pieces can step aside and let the piece behind it attack. A discovered attack, open to them. The human-move model sees an ordinary move.
The other side gets a discovered attack. The one searched move that kept the position playable was different, and the human-move model rates it hard to see.
Another move uncovered an attack, one piece stepping aside for another. The human-move model finds this move more natural. The attack stays covered.
The only searched move that held was a discovered attack. Nobody played it. The human-move model rates it a hard find.
Two demands, one move: a double attack, and the engine's best. The human-move model and the alternatives call it hard to find.
Two bills arrive at once. The human-move model would have passed it over; the engine calls it strong.
A single move with two threats behind it. The human-move model predicts it; the engine puts nothing above it.
A double attack, two threats with one move. The human-move model finds it ordinary. Strong, says the engine; not its first choice.
The other side can now make two threats with one move. A natural pick for the human-move model. Both threats will still want answers.
A double attack is now in the other side's hands. The single searched defense was elsewhere; the human-move model calls it hard to see.
Two threats at once were available to another move. The human-move model finds this one more likely, and the double attack goes unplayed.
The only searched move that held made two attacks at once. Missed. The human-move model rates it hard to see.
A defender is pulled off its post, leaving its charge open. The engine's best. The human-move model and the alternatives make it a hard find.
A deflection: the defender is pried loose from its job. Not a move the human-move model predicts. Strong, all the same, by the engine.
Lure the defender away, and its job goes undone. The human-move model expects the move. The engine ranks it first.
Deflection: the defender is hauled off what it was guarding. Expected by the human-move model; strong for the engine, with a different first choice.
The other side can now pull a defender off its job. The human-move model predicts this move. What the defender covers may come open.
A deflection is available to the other side. The defense that held was another move, the only one searched; the human-move model rates it hard to find.
A deflection was available elsewhere, a defender to be pulled off its post. The human-move model finds this one more natural. The defender stays put.
The only searched move that held was a deflection. Not played. The human-move model rates it a hard find.
The target had no guard, and the engine's best move takes it. The human-move model grades it hard to see. Loose pieces hide well.
An undefended piece, taken. An unlikely move to the human-move model, and a strong one to the engine.
Nothing guards the target, so it gets taken. Expected by the human-move model, and the engine's best. Convenient.
An undefended piece gets collected. The human-move model finds it natural; strong, by the engine, not its first choice.
Another move took a piece nothing guarded. The human-move model finds this move more natural. The loose piece survives.
The only searched move that held captured an undefended piece. Missed. The human-move model rates it hard to notice.
A piece is left unguarded, and the other side can take it. The human-move model calls the move natural. That piece remains loose.
The other side can now capture an unguarded piece. The lone searched move that held was something else; the human-move model rates it hard to see.
Off its starting square goes a minor piece. The engine ranks it best. The human-move model grades it hard to find.
A minor piece gets to work. The human-move model did not expect it; the engine rates it strong.
Development, plain and simple. The likely move for the human-move model, and the engine's first choice.
A minor piece gets developed. A likely move, to the human-move model. Strong, by the engine, which ranks another move higher.
An open file, and a rook to use it. The engine's best. The human-move model rates it hard to see.
The rook claims a file with no pawns on it. Unexpected, to the human-move model. Strong, to the engine.
Rook to an open file, clear of pawns. The human-move model and the engine land on the same move: natural, and best.
Open file, and now a rook on it. The human-move model expects it; the engine calls it strong and prefers another.
Semi-open file, rook in place: none of its own pawns, at least one of theirs. Top of the engine's search, and hard to spot for the human-move model.
The rook moves to a file free of its own pawns but not the enemy's. Low on the human-move model's list, and strong in the engine's search.
A semi-open file for the rook, clear of its own pawns. Natural for the human-move model, first for the engine.
The rook moves onto a semi-open file. The human-move model finds it ordinary. Strong for the engine, though not its first.
A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbor. The engine's best; the human-move model rates it a hard find.
Result: a passed pawn. The human-move model would have passed it over; the engine calls it strong.
A passed pawn, with no enemy pawn left to stop it on its file or the files beside it. The human-move model expects the move. The engine ranks it first.
Now there is a passed pawn. Expected by the human-move model; strong for the engine, with a different first choice.
The passed pawn edges nearer promotion. The engine's best, and a hard find by the human-move model and the alternatives searched.
Further up the board goes the passed pawn. Low on the human-move model's list, strong in the engine's search.
The passed pawn is pushed on. No disagreement: the human-move model predicts it, and the engine ranks it first.
The passed pawn moves further up the board. The human-move model would predict it. Strong, by the engine, which ranks another move higher.
This isolates a pawn, with no friendly pawn on either side of it. Still the engine's best, and the human-move model rates it a hard find.
A pawn is left isolated. Not a move the human-move model predicts. Strong, all the same, by the engine.
The engine's best move isolates a pawn; no friendly pawn on either neighboring file. The human-move model expects it too. Structure is not everything.
An isolated pawn remains. The human-move model finds the move ordinary. The engine grades it strong, but not first.
That piece is no longer on its own; it has a guard. The engine ranks it best. Hard to find, by the human-move model's reckoning.
Cover arrives for an undefended piece. Unexpected, to the human-move model. Strong, to the engine.
The loose piece is covered now. Predicted by the human-move model, ranked first by the engine.
A defender arrives for an unguarded piece. The human-move model expects it; the engine calls it strong and prefers another.
No defender left for that piece, though nothing says it can be won. Still the engine's best. The human-move model calls it a hard find.
One piece goes without a defender; that alone proves nothing. The human-move model did not expect the move. The engine grades it strong.
Even the engine's best move leaves a piece undefended here, and undefended is not lost. The human-move model expects the move.
A piece goes undefended, though not lost. The human-move model finds the move natural; strong, by the engine, not its first choice.
The king gets a legal flight square out of this. The engine's best, and the human-move model and the searched alternatives put it among the hard finds.
A new escape square for the king. Low on the human-move model's list, and strong in the engine's search.
The king gains breathing room: a legal square to step to. The human-move model predicts it; the engine puts nothing above it.
An escape square for the king, where there was none. Likely, by the human-move model. Strong, by the engine, which ranks another move higher.
Castled, rook and king both repositioned. The engine's best. Here, the human-move model calls it a hard find.
Castling, and the rook joins the game. The human-move model did not expect castling here; the engine rates it strong.
The king castles here. The likely move for the human-move model, and the engine's first choice.
Castling: two pieces moved for one tempo. The human-move model finds it ordinary. Strong, says the engine; not its first choice.
With this capture, the other side's bishop pair is finished. The engine's best; the human-move model rates it a hard find.
This capture splits the opposing bishops; the pair is finished. The human-move model would have passed it over; the engine calls it strong.
